title: Run, schedule, or use events to trigger a pipeline (Fabric Data Factory)

claims.text: A pipeline run is one execution instance of a pipeline and can be started three ways: on demand from the editor, on a time-based schedule, or from an event trigger that fires on occurrences such as files arriving in storage.

Fabric pipeline schedules have no open-ended option: every schedule requires both a start and an end date, so long-running pipelines are kept alive by setting an end date far in the future and adjusting it later.
A single pipeline can carry up to 20 schedules, each with its own frequency, start/end dates, and time zone, which lets one pipeline serve several delivery cadences without duplication.

Interval-based schedules (in public preview) run a pipeline over fixed, non-overlapping time windows and inject two trigger parameters, window start time and window end time, into the pipeline expression builder, enabling time-sliced incremental processing patterns.

Interval-based schedules currently cannot be edited, enabled, or disabled after creation (they must be deleted and recreated), and time-slice monitoring and backfill are not yet available for them, which limits their use for production windowed loads that need replay.

Schedules can pass parameter values into the pipeline at each run, sourced either as a direct static value or as a reference into a variable library, the latter centralizing configuration for promotion across environments.

Parameter names configured on a schedule must match the pipeline's parameter names exactly; a mismatched name is silently ignored at run time rather than raising an error, so typos produce defaults instead of failures.

Email failure notifications can be configured per schedule by adding users or groups, but they fire only for scheduled runs, never for on-demand runs, so manual test executions will not alert anyone on failure.

Event-based pipeline triggers are built on Fabric platform plumbing rather than a bespoke trigger service: defining a storage event trigger creates an eventstream object plus a Data Activator alert stored as a Reflex item in the workspace, and triggers can respond to file events, job events, and workspace events.

Pipeline storage-event triggers in Data Factory consume Real-Time Intelligence components: the event flow runs through an eventstream and the trigger rule lives in Data Activator, so trigger management happens partly in those experiences rather than only in the pipeline editor.

Storage event triggers can listen to OneLake events or Azure Blob Storage events, and event filtering on files and folders is expressed against the event's Subject field, since file name and folder path are encoded inside Subject rather than as separate properties.

Trigger metadata such as the triggering file name reaches pipeline expressions via parameters parsed from the event's Subject and Topic fields, referenced with null-safe syntax like @pipeline()?.TriggerEvent?.FileName, because during a manual test run these values are NULL and an unguarded reference would fail.

The storage events delivered to triggers follow the CloudEvents schema (specversion 1.0) with top-level properties including source, subject, type, time, id, and a data payload object supplied by Event Grid.
